items.question: What do you see as an important flaw in how tokenization handles different languages?
items.object: Tokenization’s unequal compression rates across languages
items.answer: I think probably the more important reason tokenization is kind of flawed is that there are different compression rates for different languages and scripts. High resource languages like English are totally fine: on average a token is maybe four or five characters, or approximately a word. But for other languages, the same sentence could be tokenized into so many tokens. Users who speak those languages, when they interact with language model APIs where users are charged per token, they'll be overcharged, basically.

items.question: Why did you find natural language processing an appealing focus within computer science?
items.object: Natural language processing as a marriage of linguistics and computer science
items.answer: Throughout college I kind of wasn't sure about what topic within computer science was really my focus. I thought I could have been a systems person or a theory person for a long time. But the thing that brought me toward machine learning was taking my first linguistics class. I really enjoyed looking at language in a different way that I hadn't before. Linguistics really approaches studying language as a science as well, and marrying linguistics and computer science—natural language processing—is the most natural way to do that, the perfect marriage of the two. So that's what got me interested in NLP.

items.question: How do you see language models changing the questions you can ask about human language?
items.object: Language models as tools for understanding linguistics and cognitive science
items.answer: Another big strand of my research, the focus of the Mission: Impossible paper as well as follow-ups we're doing to that paper, is looking at how language models could help us understand linguistics or cognitive science. It used to be the case where we just wanted computers to be able to mimic human language in some way, but now that they're so good, the question is: can they help us learn more about language?

items.question: How do you think about the tradeoffs of tokenization in large language models?
items.object: Tokenization in large language models
items.answer:
I think of tokenization as a form of compression. It's the preprocessing step that's central to basically every language model that you've heard of these days. It breaks up text into chunks or units called tokens. You can think of these as words or parts of words, and these are the units that we feed into a language model.

It's basically taking a long text sequence and making it into a smaller set of units. If you think about the Transformer, the component that's really central to all of the large language models that we know today, it can be very expensive. The term here is quadratic complexity in terms of the sequence length for the attention mechanism. Long sequences are pretty inefficient, and tokenization compresses them into these smaller units.

However, there are some big problems with tokenization. For one, it can be really sensitive to character manipulations or character level noise. A simple spelling error can result in a sequence being represented by a completely different set of tokens. Probably the more important reason tokenization is kind of flawed is that there are different compression rates for different languages and scripts. High resource languages like English are totally fine: on average a token is maybe four or five characters, or approximately a word. But for other languages, the same sentence could be tokenized into so many tokens, basically operating at a character level, so then all the problems of efficiency come in. Users who speak those languages, when they interact with language model APIs where users are charged per token, they'll be overcharged, basically. I think the unfairness aspect is really interesting to me.

items.question: How do you reconcile tokenization’s sensitivity to character errors with the ability of large language models to understand sloppy input?
items.object: Tokenization’s sensitivity to character errors in large language models
items.answer:
Intuitively, when I think about tokenization and how it's sensitive to character errors, I wouldn't necessarily want two words that are spelled slightly differently—if a word is spelled slightly differently, it can be chunked in a different way. Or maybe if a letter is capital, then that word will get a completely different input representation, and the model basically has to learn that, “Oh, this word that you meant actually means this other word.” It has to kind of learn that implicitly.

I think the models are just trained on a ton of data and trained for very long, so maybe these differences don't seem to matter as much on the surface. But I think that it can still result in weird, interesting failure cases in certain points.

items.question: Why do you think subword tokenization can be inefficient for Arabic even beyond the amount of Arabic in the tokenizer’s training data?
items.object: Subword tokenization’s efficiency for Arabic
items.answer:
I have this example when I give talks about Mr. T: I take the GPT-4 tokenizer and have a sentence in English and its translation in Arabic. We know that these sentences mean the same exact thing because it's literally the same sentence, just translated into Arabic. The exact number I have for the GPT-4 tokenizer on that language is that the English sentence is tokenized into 10 tokens or so, or nine tokens, and then the Arabic sentence is tokenized into 31 tokens, even though there are actually fewer characters in the Arabic sequence.

There are a variety of factors that go into this. Perhaps it's just that the tokenizer is not trained on enough Arabic, or maybe English is the dominant language. But also, from a linguistic perspective, Arabic is one of those languages where meaningful units are not necessarily adjacent. These things are called infixes in languages. Rather than putting a prefix or a suffix, like we do in English to add meaning to a word, where you put “-ed” to make the past tense, you can shove it in the middle of a word. Now it's no longer concatenating something to the end; it's inserting it in the middle. The way the morphology works is actually breaking the word into pieces. From a linguistic perspective, I can see why an algorithm that is kind of merging frequent adjacent tokens might not be the best for all languages, beyond just having enough data for that language during tokenizer training.

items.question: How do you weigh the benefits and drawbacks of character-level or byte-level language models compared with subword tokenization?
items.object: Character-level and byte-level language modeling
items.answer: Most of the main models use subword tokenization, which is what we've talked about. The alternative would be character-level or byte-level models. These language models don't perform a tokenization preprocessing step; they just take in the raw character or byte sequences as the units that the Transformer, or the language model, will operate on. The benefit here is that some of the issues that we talked about, like sensitivity to character-level manipulations or the model having more awareness of what characters comprise its tokens, are addressed by modeling at the character or byte level. The issue is that you still get problems of having very long sequence lengths when you're just operating on the raw character or byte streams.

items.question: Why did you choose ByT5 as the starting point for your work on making byte-level language models more efficient?
items.object: ByT5 as a starting point for improving byte-level model efficiency
items.answer: There are different architectures that have addressed this. In the related work section, I talk about Charformer, or CANINE, Google's character-level counterpart to multilingual. There are different architectures to try and downsample the sequence in a learned way. The focus of our paper is on ByT5, and the reason we focused on ByT5 is it had very impressive performance compared to its token-level counterpart, which was mT5. On all these benchmarks, it matched or even outperformed mT5. But the main problem was efficiency: it was exactly the architecture of mT5, but operating on bytes, so you get these very long sequence lengths. Our idea was, how can we take this existing byte-level model and make it more efficient, specifically through minimal fine-tuning? That's where the idea started.

items.question: How do you view soft tokenization methods in relation to the preprocessing tokenization used by most language models?
items.object: Soft tokenization methods
items.answer: I'm pro those methods. There are methods that some would call soft tokenization, which is maybe you feed in a character or byte sequence, but the Transformer learns how to group tokens implicitly via some learned mechanism. An example would be the Charformer architecture, or another example is our Glassing Transformer, which we also partially replicate in the paper. Some call those soft tokenization. I would consider that separate from the typical subword tokenization that we know about in most language models, like your Llamas or your GPT.

items.question: How did your thinking about what prevents character- and byte-level language models from taking off shape your research direction?
items.object: Efficiency as a barrier to adopting character- and byte-level language models
items.answer: Actually, how this project came about was I was just exploring doing some interpretability work on character-level language models: what do models learn about words when they're operating at the character level or the byte level? I was in a meeting with my advisers, Chris Potts and Dan Jurafsky, and I think we just came to a point where we said, “Why aren't people using these models? If there are these benefits to abandoning subword tokenization, what's preventing them from taking off?” It seems like the main thing is the efficiency aspect, so I geared toward an architecture project that could address that.

items.question: How do you think about Mr. T5's approach to deciding which byte or character tokens to drop?
items.object: Mr. T5's token-dropping architecture
items.answer:
The idea we kind of came up with is, maybe after a couple of contextual layers of the model, after you've processed this entire byte or character sequence through a couple of encoder layers, tokens already contain information about other tokens via the attention mechanism. Then the model can decide what tokens it can drop and what tokens can remain to be processed by the rest of the encoder layers. That's the main idea.

The way we do this is with a gating mechanism that learns to drop tokens and learns which ones to keep as well. The gating mechanism does the work of deciding which tokens will be removed from the sequence. The way I like to think of it is that during training, Mr. T5 is doing this dropping as an attention masking process. To describe what attention masking is, it's a process that we use in language models to prevent certain tokens from looking at other tokens during the attention computation. The typical uses are, in a decoder model, you don't want preceding tokens to be able to look into the future because that would defeat the purpose of next token prediction, so you would mask out future tokens. In an encoder model, you might have sequences of different lengths, so when you process them in a batch you pad them up, and you want to mask out the pad tokens because you wouldn't want them to affect the representations of other tokens.

The way we do this in Mr. T5 is: can the model learn which tokens to mask out via a learned attention masking mechanism? That's what we do during training. The model has a learned attention masking function that removes tokens from the sequence during training, or doesn't allow the tokens that remain to look at the other tokens for most of the encoder layers. During inference is when we actually remove those tokens from the sequence in what we call a hard deletion mechanism. Those tokens are actually removed from the sequence, and the sequence length is resized into a shorter, more compact sequence.

items.question: How do you understand the role of early-layer attention in making dynamic token merging possible?
items.object: Dynamic token merging through early-layer attention
items.answer: The idea of merging is that we allow the model to kind of— the attention mechanism of early layers already does a sort of merging, because every unit or every token, through attention, is a combination of the tokens around it. Information has already been merged to other tokens in the early layers, and maybe some of them could be dropped now because they've merged their information into other tokens.

items.question: What do you find interesting about how Mr. T5 learns to compress different languages?
items.object: Mr. T5's learned language-specific compression rates
items.answer:
In our main experiments, we train Mr. T5 on multilingual data, sampling 15 different languages from multilingual C4 for our continued pretraining experiments. We don't give Mr. T5 a certain prior to compress languages at different compression rates. We have this formulation where, using this controller algorithm that's detailed in the paper, we can target a specific compression rate if desired. Let's say I want Mr. T5 to compress sequences by 50% on average; Mr. T5 will do that.

When I tested on individual languages separately, we actually found that Mr. T5 learns language-specific compression rates. For example, Chinese, which already has a very information-dense script—individual characters could mean entire words; that's just how the orthography of Chinese is—Mr. T5 had a lower compression rate for Chinese than for other Latin-script languages. It kind of already notices that Chinese is pretty compressed, so it's not going to compress it as much as a language that uses another script that is not as compressed. I thought that was super interesting because we're not injecting that prior; it just learns it implicitly.

items.question: What do you find significant about Mr. T5’s performance on the multilingual benchmarks XNLI and TyDi QA?
items.object: Mr. T5’s performance on multilingual benchmarks
items.answer:
In the section on downstream fine-tuning in the paper, we fine-tune on some additional tasks. From the ByT5 paper, we look at the XNLI and TyDi QA tasks. Those are both multilingual benchmarks. XNLI is a classification task: natural language inference is kind of like you take two sentences and need to determine whether they entail, contradict each other, or if there's no relationship. TyDi QA is a question-answering task: given a passage and a question, can the model retrieve the answer from it? These are both multilingual, so it tests the multilingual capabilities of Mr. T5 as well.

We found that Mr. T5 can reduce sequence lengths on those tasks, I think up to 45 or 50%, while maintaining close to the same performance as ByT5. I think even for XNLI it outperformed ByT5, which was interesting because you would think that ByT5, since we're fine-tuning on top of ByT5, would present a bound on how good you can get. Mr. T5 could match the performance while significantly speeding up the model.

items.question: How do you interpret Mr. T5’s results on character-level spelling correction and word search tasks?
items.object: Character-level tasks as a test of Mr. T5’s compression
items.answer:
We also tested on some character-level manipulations. We took two tasks from a character-level benchmark: a spelling correction task and a word search task. The spelling correction task is, given a sentence that contains some spelling error, can you reproduce the sentence but corrected? The word search task is, given a random sequence of a bunch of characters or numbers, can you find the English word that matches some definition? Subword models are really bad at these two tasks. This comes from a benchmark created by another PhD student in my lab, Jing Huang. She evaluated subword T5 and compared it to ByT5 at the time, before Mr. T5, and the subword models really struggle on these sorts of character-level tasks.

Back to our paper, Mr. T5 is able to significantly reduce the sequence lengths and improve the runtime while coming close to matching ByT5's performance on the task. So you get the benefits of the compression without an effect on the model's performance.

items.question: How do you understand the conditions under which Mr. T5 delivers the greatest inference efficiency gains over ByT5?
items.object: Mr. T5’s inference efficiency relative to ByT5
items.answer: The task efficiency will vary depending on how big the encoder sequence lengths are relative to the decoder. If you have very long encoder sequence lengths and very short decoder sequence lengths, you're going to get the most gains. I think we saw the most gains on the XNLI task because the encoder sequences are very long and then the decoder is just a classification task, so you're outputting a number. items.question: Why do you think scaling byte-level language models could help explain why they haven't caught on?
items.object: Scaling byte-level language models
items.answer:
While this is particularly an architecture that enhances ByT5, if we had the resources to train from scratch or train at large scales, maybe the benefits would be even greater—I bet the benefits would be even greater. One of the results that we have in the new version of the paper is training a larger, 1.2 billion parameter model and seeing how the efficiency gains are even greater at that scale. This makes me think about whether, if we could scale these models up as much as we've scaled up subword-level models, maybe we could get back to the problem of why these haven't caught on. Maybe we just haven't scaled them up enough to that point.

I should mention a new paper from Meta, the Byte Latent Transformer, that scaled up byte-level models to 8 billion parameters. They had a particular architecture, trained from scratch, and found that it matched their Llama model—I think it was Llama 2 that they compared to.

items.question: How do you view the potential for byte-level modeling to replace subword token-level modeling?
items.object: Byte-level modeling as a potential replacement for subword token-level modeling
items.answer: I think it's hard to tell the future, but I think it's very promising. Not even just the issues that I talked about previously, but maybe there are sequences that could be compressed more that a token-level model doesn't compress. There are some very predictable sequences that I could imagine I wouldn't want a Transformer to spend so much time operating on. Let's say I give it a sequence that's like “To be or not to be, that is the question.” I know what that is, and maybe the model knows that's a very predictable sequence. Maybe spending several tokens to process that—whereas maybe a byte-level model or another model that uses some sort of downsampling could compress that whole sequence into one unit. I could see how the efficiency gains might even be better than a subword model. I think these ideas started to be explored more in the Byte Latent Transformer paper, but I'd love to see character-level models and other architectures scaled up, including Mr. T.

items.question: Why do you see dynamic compression as a bigger benefit than fixed-length downsampling in character-level models?
items.object: Dynamic compression versus fixed-length downsampling in character-level models
items.answer: Dynamic compression is the big benefit there. Other models that maybe do fixed-length downsampling—I don't see as much. Maybe every four characters are going to chunk into one representation. That still has benefits of being more character-aware, because maybe you're pooling over representations of characters, but it's still not dynamic in a way that you would get those sorts of benefits of actually being able to compress really long sequences into fewer representations.

items.question: What drew you to the research problem behind your Mission: Impossible paper?
items.object: The research motivation behind the Mission: Impossible paper
items.answer: I remember I was just starting off and talking to my adviser Chris Potts about potential first research topics. We had both read the New York Times op-ed where Noam Chomsky, a very famous and very important linguist, talked about language models and whether they have a bearing on studying linguistics. His argument in the New York Times article was that language models learned too much. They're too good, to the point where they could learn impossible languages, which are languages that humans wouldn't be able to learn. From a research perspective, I thought this would be a really cool problem to explore.

items.question: How do you understand Noam Chomsky's argument that language models' ability to learn undermines their usefulness as models of human language?
items.object: Noam Chomsky's critique of language models as tools for studying human language
items.answer: I think that's the core idea of a lot of his critiques of language up to this point. This particular point was how even how good language models are is detrimental to their use as models of language or as linguistic tools, because they couldn't possibly match certain human behaviors just because of how well they learn. I think that was his main point in that article.

items.question: What research opportunity did you see in Mitchell and Bowers's paper on impossible languages?
items.object: Mitchell and Bowers's computational research on impossible languages
items.answer: I would consider it one of the first papers to explore impossible languages from a computational lens. That paper was really cool, but we thought we could expand to more languages and also test on more modern architectures. Rather than the recurrent neural networks they tested in that paper, we could also test on Transformer-based language models, which are at the core of language models today. Chris and I were both really excited about the topic. He remembers thinking it was maybe too ambitious of a project for a first project, but I remember him being very positive and supportive of pursuing this direction.

items.question: How do you think about the difficulty of defining an impossible language?
items.object: Defining and testing impossible languages
items.answer:
I don't think that there is a very clear answer still. Truthfully, there's not a very clear answer, because the definition of an impossible language is a language that a human wouldn't be able to learn. It would be very unethical, I think, to try out different languages on babies. That's the ideal thing, right? All of the languages that we test on, we'd want to be able to give to a baby and see if the baby would be able to learn it, but we can't do that for obvious reasons.

In the paper, we take perspectives from linguistic theory as well as perspectives that are more from the ML side, of languages that have inherently more entropy and would be more difficult for both a human and a machine learning algorithm. We try to test on a broad range of languages in the paper. These go from languages that are very intuitively impossible, like languages that involved random shuffling of words within sentences. That sounds fun, sounds intuitively impossible, but we even had to hedge there. We included a footnote: we believe that these languages are impossible given the context where we're scrambling English words. But there are some languages in the world called scrambling languages or free word order languages, where words can appear in almost any order, but usually there's some other process in the language that disambiguates the meaning in a different way.

items.question: What do you find interesting about the counting-based “hop” languages you created by perturbing English?
items.object: Counting-based “hop” languages created by perturbing English
items.answer:
I think the main set of languages in the paper that we focus on are these “hop” languages. These are inspired a bit by some artificial language learning experiments that have been done on humans about how humans disprefer languages that involve certain counting-based rules. In the languages that we have in the paper, basically we take English—all of our languages involve perturbing English. To talk about these hop languages, we take verbs and remove any sort of inflection, meaning how you mark tense or number, and we put a marker that signifies tense and number four words later. That doesn't sound inherently too complex, but it's something that no language really does, having this verb inflection be marked by a marker that comes four words after a verb.

I remember it sounds like it should be pretty easy for a language model. We have some targeted evaluations showing that the model is actually more surprised by those markers, or is worse at predicting those markers, than in a control condition where the marker appears right next to the verb, as it would in the natural English setting. We thought that was pretty interesting.

items.question: How do you explain GPT-2’s greater difficulty learning the impossible languages in your experiments?
items.object: GPT-2's bias toward natural language and information locality
items.answer: The main takeaway there was that, at least for the class of models we tested—like the GPT-2 models we trained from scratch—we had to train all the models from scratch on each impossible language. These models are not pretrained on top of massive English corpora; they only see their respective impossible languages. There's something about the GPT-2 architecture that biases it toward the natural language, meaning the control languages in our experiments. That's kind of the main takeaway. Our thought was that it has to do with—our hypothesis is that the GPT-2 architecture prefers information locality. What this basically means is that in language, words that are predictive of each other are often close together. When we mess with the locality of a language, that's what makes it harder for GPT-2, and we think it comes from the autoregressive language modeling objective, where the language model has to predict the next token given the preceding tokens.

items.question: Why do you think the BabyLM corpus is a good starting point for your experiments with impossible languages?
items.object: The BabyLM corpus for controlled language learning experiments
items.answer:
We started off from an English corpus. This is a BabyLM corpus, about 100 million words of text. It's supposed to be approximately what a child would hear up to age 12. I think it's a nice corpus if you're trying to do these sorts of language learning experiments. It also is supposed to mimic what a child would encounter during the first 12 years of life.

What we did was define rules that would transform the English corpus into each impossible language. The data is very controlled when we compare each impossible language: it's the same sentences that have just been transformed by different rules. That's how we went about it, and then we pretrained the GPT-2s on each corpus.

items.question: How do you see changes to GPT-2's architecture helping make it a more cognitively plausible model of language?
items.object: Language model architecture as a source of cognitive plausibility
items.answer: The architecture question is what we think would be a really natural next step: how can we find architectures that are more biased toward the natural languages and less biased toward the impossible languages? Ultimately, all of the parts of GPT-2 are engineering choices, and there's no reason we can't just change them in order to make them more cognitively plausible models. These are great directions, and I'm excited that people are working on them more. In the follow-up, we're working more on the architecture question. That's what we're targeting in Mission: Impossible 2, continuing the theme of the pop culture reference in the title.

items.question: How do you see the connection between your Mr. T and Mission: Impossible papers?
items.object: Architecture exploration across Mr. T and Mission: Impossible
items.answer:
I'm continuing to be very excited in tokenization and very excited in architectures. The link between the two papers that I talked about is the exploration of what is learnable and what architectures are best for your specific use cases. For Mr. T, it's obviously what architecture is going to be best for achieving more efficient byte-level models. For Mission: Impossible, I think the next clear step is to explore the architectures that make a learner more or less biased toward natural or impossible language.

I'm just really excited to do more work on architecture. I think these two questions have allowed me to explore that, especially in a world where the standard Transformer architecture is very dominant. I've been very happy to break away from that a bit.
